Ignition timing is adjusted by the ignition system, not represented by octane rating.
Combustion temperature is not what the octane number rates.
Fuel delivery from tanks is handled by the fuel system; the carburettor mixes fuel and air.
The throttle affects power by controlling airflow, but that is not the carburettor's overall task.
Additional cooling fuel can be a mixture effect, not the carburettor's major task.
The carburettor's main purpose is to produce a combustible air/fuel mixture for the engine.
The bank's most-likely range is −5°C to +20°C; icing is possible with cool, moist air.
This option includes colder temperatures but omits the bank's +10°C to +20°C range.
The bank's keyed range extends to +20°C, beyond this option's +5°C limit.
The bank's range begins at −5°C, not −15°C, and extends above zero.
80-109.note: (bank key) The keyed range is a likelihood cue, not a hard boundary; carburettor icing can occur across broader conditions.

80-110.topic: Oil, cooling, engine instruments and propeller
why: The bank's CHT reading is associated with the critical cylinder, not every cylinder.
It is not a random cylinder; the instrument monitors the selected critical cylinder.
CHT indication is for the critical cylinder in the bank's description.
A critical-cylinder reading is not the average temperature of all cylinders.
Piston helicopter engines normally have dual ignition, not one magneto system.
The two ignition systems are not simply one electrical ignition system.
The systems are independent, not coupled together as a single ignition system.
Two independent ignition systems provide redundancy, commonly through separate magnetos and plugs.

80-112.topic: Oil, cooling, engine instruments and propeller
why: The blade angle between chord and plane of rotation is its angle of incidence/pitch.
Angle of attack is between chord and local airflow, not the plane of rotation.
Geometric twist is a spanwise change in blade angle, not this local angle.
Aerodynamic twist is not the angle between blade chord and rotation plane.

80-113.topic: Oil, cooling, engine instruments and propeller
why: Power increase is not begun by decreasing manifold pressure.
RPM should be increased before manifold pressure, not decreased first.
The bank's safe increase sequence is RPM first, then manifold pressure/throttle.
Increasing RPM after manifold pressure risks high MAP at low RPM; reverse the order.

80-114.topic: Oil, cooling, engine instruments and propeller
why: Reduce manifold pressure first, then reduce RPM; this order starts with the wrong control.
Increasing RPM while reducing power is not the required two-step sequence.
The bank sequence reduces manifold pressure first, then RPM; this option reverses it.
Power decrease sequence is throttle/MAP down first, followed by RPM down.
A naturally aspirated carburettor engine loses power as air density falls with altitude.
Power does not begin increasing above 5,000 ft; reduced air mass lowers output.
Increasing altitude reduces available air and engine power, rather than increasing it.
With altitude, less air enters a naturally aspirated engine, so power decreases.
With ignition switched OFF, RPM falls, then returns to its former value on BOTH.
A grounded magneto switch cuts ignition briefly, reducing RPM; BOTH restores the original value.
RPM falls when OFF rather than increasing, then recovers on BOTH.
When switched back to BOTH, RPM should return to the previous value, not remain lower.
Each listed instrument senses pressure, including oil/fuel/MAP, altimeter, VSI, ASI and suction.
Fuel quantity is a level/quantity measurement, not pressure; this set includes it.
Directional gyro and turn coordinator are gyro instruments, not pressure-measuring devices.
The magnetic compass is magnetic, not pressure-operated; the other examples include pressure instruments.
A flight level is an altitude surface referenced to standard pressure, i.e. pressure altitude.
Density altitude corrects pressure altitude for temperature, not the definition of a flight level.
A flight level is not a height above ground; it uses the standard pressure datum.
True altitude is corrected for temperature; a flight level is based on standard pressure.
In colder-than-ISA air, true altitude is lower than indicated; the indication is too high.
The indicated altitude is not lower; cold air makes the aircraft's true altitude lower than indicated.
Cold-temperature error means indicated and true altitude are not equal.
Standard altitude is a pressure reference, not the cold-air true-altitude relationship.
At ISA temperature with QNH set, indicated altitude is approximately true altitude.
Correct QNH at ISA makes indicated altitude equal to true, not lower.
ISA is the temperature condition, not the altitude reading's definition.
With correct QNH and ISA conditions, the altimeter does not over-read true altitude.
A pulled circuit breaker may disable equipment but does not normally alter sensed airspeed.
An earth/bond wire left attached does not by itself cause erroneous airspeed indication.
A boost-pressure line is not the ASI's pitot-static pressure input.
Adhesive covering can disrupt pitot/static airflow or ports and cause erroneous ASI indication.
The yellow arc is the caution range for smooth air, not the red-line limit.
Flap-extended speed is VFE at the white-arc limit, not the red range.
The red line indicates VNE, never-exceed speed under any circumstances.
The red limit does not apply only to turns above a specified bank angle.
Deviation is caused by aircraft magnetic fields, not Earth's dip angle.
Acceleration produces compass error, but dip is caused by magnetic-field inclination.
Dip error results from inclination of Earth's magnetic field lines to the horizontal.
Temperature variation is not the cause of compass dip error.
Gyroscopic precession is approximately 90°, not 45°, from the applied force.
Precession direction depends on gyro rotation and applied force, not simply north.
A spinning gyro responds about 90° from an applied force in the direction of rotation.
A 180° response is opposite the force, not the gyro's precession rule.
The bank requires a serviceable airspeed indicator; GPS groundspeed is not a substitute.
GPS shows groundspeed, not required airspeed, and does not replace a failed ASI.
Availability of a maintenance organisation does not make an unserviceable ASI acceptable.
Restricting flight to circuits does not remove the required airspeed indication.
An ADI combines the attitude indicator with flight-director command information.
Directional and rate gyros are not the ADI's defining combination.
A relative-bearing indicator is not part of the ADI combination.
An RMI is not the ADI's flight-director command component.
HSI expands to Horizontal Situation Indicator.
Hybernating System Indication is not an aviation instrument acronym.
Horizontal Slip Indicator is not the expansion of HSI.
This humorous phrase is not the accepted instrument name.
Winglets are not primarily used to increase gliding performance at high speed.
Winglets do not increase lift or turning manoeuvring capability as their purpose.
They may improve effective aspect ratio, but the bank's direct aerodynamic effect is reduced induced drag.
Winglets weaken wingtip vortices and reduce induced drag.
